name: Cryptography and Security

papers.title: Demystifying Real-world LLM Service Freeloading
papers.abstract: Third-party projects repackage free inference from LLM web applications and dedicated clients into independent APIs. We refer to such use beyond providers' permitted access, allocation, or redistribution conditions as LLM service freeloading (LSF). However, its scale and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We present a systematic measurement study of 513 open-source projects, tracing 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream LLM services and characterizing their development, dependencies, and operating mechanisms. We find that 93.0% of repositories were created in 2026. Direct HTTP or WebSocket requests account for 83.2% of paths, making reproduction of product protocols the dominant invocation method. Projects adapt messages, reconstruct conversation state, and convert responses to support compatible APIs. Account selection or rotation appears on 304 paths (19.1%), allowing projects with multiple eligible accounts to distribute requests across their separate allowances. Our policy analysis finds that 58 of the 62 services with available terms explicitly prohibit at least one examined practice, including automated access, account sharing, or service redistribution. These restrictions cover both downstream API provision and the means of obtaining upstream inference. Our findings inform defenses against unauthorized consumption and redistribution of free LLM resources. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to the relevant providers.

papers.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
papers.abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.

papers.title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection
papers.abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.

papers.title: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further shows that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.

papers.title: RegionAlign: Manipulating Parameter Layouts for Localized Fault Injection on LLMs and VLMs
papers.abstract: Physical fault injection can flip stored weight bits, degrading LLMs and VLMs. Existing work largely overlooks how supply-chain manipulation affects fault vulnerability. We introduce RegionAlign, which allows a malicious provider to manipulate only the parameter layout before deployment, using bit-sensitivity search and channel permutations to concentrate vulnerable bits in one memory region while preserving weight values and clean performance. Under matched budgets, software experiments show greater degradation from search-selected in-region flips with RegionAlign than with original or random layouts. EMFI feasibility study confirms weight corruption. RegionAlign reveals a stealthy supply-chain threat that layout manipulation weakens physical fault resilience.

papers.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination
papers.abstract: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.

papers.title: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving defenses improve LLM-agent security by learning reusable policies from observed attacks. However, we demonstrate that this learning process itself can become an attack surface. Using SED (Self-Evolving Defense) in the AgentDojo benchmark, we construct a single prompt-injection episode that causes the defense to learn an over-broad policy and subsequently refuse legitimate requests. Across 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refuses at least one legitimate task, while unrelated-task performance remains unchanged and the original prompt-injection defense remains effective. The attack also transfers to gpt-oss-120b; however, its poisoning mechanism depends on a successful initial prompt injection and therefore fails to activate when the target agent resists the underlying injection. In contrast, integrity-oriented attacks targeting SED's judge, policy synthesis, retrieval, and organization mechanisms fail in our evaluated settings, identifying over-refusal as the primary exploitable failure mode observed in our experiments. We further identify self-poisoning from false-positive harm judgments without an attacker. Finally, contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate over-refusal, without compromising security in our evaluated settings.

papers.title: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of modern hardware designs is making security assurance increasingly difficult. One of the foundational steps in pre-silicon security verification is identifying security assets. While primary assets are often evident from design functionality, the internal signals that can facilitate their compromise are much less apparent. Complex data- and control-flow dependencies create many such internal security-critical locations, whose exploitation depends on the threat-specific attack mechanism---these are the secondary assets. To precisely identify these, we propose SecID, a multi-agent framework that combines deterministic RTL analysis with bounded dynamic evaluation and LLM reasoning to identify threat-specific secondary assets. Each asset decision is supported by functional influence, threat features, and explicit attack mechanisms. We demonstrate SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P. The experimental results are corroborated through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis, and further evaluated through pipeline- and final-stage ablation, threshold-sensitivity studies, and final-stage repeatability analysis. Together, these evaluations show that SecID can identify highly threat-relevant secondary assets with respect to a given primary asset, providing a scalable path toward hardware-security verification.

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries
papers.abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used to discover real-world security vulnerabilities, making it critical to systematically evaluate their cybersecurity capabilities. However, existing security benchmarks primarily focus on known vulnerabilities in open-source projects, largely overlooking closed-source binaries, which underpin much of the software industry. In this paper, we ask: how effective are frontier models at uncovering deep vulnerabilities in production binaries? To answer this question, we present DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in Windows kernel binaries. Given a target binary, an agent analyzes it using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated VMs and reports each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept (PoC). Unlike existing benchmarks, DeepBinary replays every report on fresh VMs and employs an LLM-based judge to assess its validity, uniqueness, and impact (estimated by bug bounty values). Beyond known vulnerabilities, DeepBinary also enables the discovery and validation of previously unknown (0-day) vulnerabilities. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of representative open- and closed-weight models (including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) across diverse coding agents (including Codex and Claude Code) on 12 target binaries. In total, they discover over 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct previously unknown vulnerabilities across all experiments. Our results further reveal substantial differences in models' ability to analyze binaries, conduct experiments, and sustain vulnerability discovery over long horizons. Overall, DeepBinary makes long-horizon, open-ended vulnerability discovery in complex binaries measurable, revealing fundamental differences in how frontier models analyze and explore such systems.

papers.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
papers.abstract: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations. We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $\Omega_{\theta}(\log n)$, where $\theta$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.

papers.title: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles
papers.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly write and submit code with limited human review, and much of it passes functional tests while remaining insecure. We show that these failures persist. Across 14 task sequences, Codex, Claude Code, and Qwen Code fixed a vulnerability 85.7% of the time when shown the failing security test, then reintroduced the same vulnerability class in a new session 26.7% of the time, about as often as agents that had never seen it (27.5%). The capability is present; the retention is not. Neither recording the repair in the agent's persistent context nor supplying published secure coding principles closed the gap: the recorded fix stayed tied to the family of the task it came from, and the principles, written for human developers, remained too general to apply to the code at hand. The knowledge exists; it is not activated. We call the missing ability security self-improvement: an agent learns from its own security failures so that each lesson persists across sessions, applies to new code, and does not break what works. We present PRECEPT, which equips coding agents with this ability through an evolving library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them against the agent's own failures, so that each principle comes to fire on the code where that agent actually goes wrong. A revision is kept only if fresh executions show it makes code more secure while keeping functional success within a small tolerance of the agent without the library. Improvement continues across evolution steps rather than saturating after the first. On task families never seen during evolution, PRECEPT's weakest agent reaches 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent at 81.9% and the strongest baseline at 87.7%.

papers.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
papers.abstract: Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from $2^{128}$ to $n \cdot 2^{128/n}$, bottoming out at $2^{12}$ for $n=16$---a factor of $2^{116}$ reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.

papers.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.

papers.title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
papers.abstract: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.

papers.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
papers.abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

papers.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
papers.abstract: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.

papers.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.

papers.title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
papers.abstract: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $\mu$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.

papers.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds. In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.

papers.title: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.

papers.title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67$\times$ more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.

papers.title: Northstar: Efficient Verifiable Negacyclic Polynomial Arithmetic with Applications to Encrypted Lattice-based Multi-Asset ERC-20 and Verifiable FHE
papers.abstract: Lattice-based cryptography can be used to construct a variety of post-quantum cryptographic schemes, ranging from standard cryptographic primitives such as digital signatures and encryption, to fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). However, the verification of correct lattice computations remains relatively expensive, particularly for computationally intensive FHE operations and for resource-constrained environments such as on-chain verification via smart contracts. We propose Northstar, an efficient technique for proving negacyclic arithmetic natively. When integrated with existing STARK proving frameworks, Northstar achieves the best overall performance across prover time, verifier time, and proof size compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches for verifiable FHE constructions. Furthermore, Northstar is used to construct the first verifiable encrypted multi-asset (~ 1000 assets) variant of ERC-20 that is efficiently verifiable by a smart contract, and is practically deployable in the current blockchain ecosystem.

papers.title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise
papers.abstract: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.

papers.title: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
papers.abstract: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.

papers.title: BridgeHammer: DNN Backdoor Attack via CPU-iGPU Shared-memory Rowhammer
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous systems-on-chips (SoCs) share physical memory between CPUs and integrated GPUs (iGPUs), creating a path for CPU-side memory corruption to compromise the integrity of deep learning models used for iGPU inference. Implanting a backdoor that causes targeted misclassifications on trigger-bearing inputs while retaining accuracy on normal inputs requires carefully selected weight changes. However, realizing these changes presents two challenges: where to induce faults, since vulnerable DRAM locations may not contain the targeted weights, and when to intervene, since memory placement and fault injection must align with different stages of the model deployment lifecycle that involve two distinct computation domains. We present BridgeHammer, a Rowhammer-based backdoor attack that addresses these challenges by coordinating targeted weight placement before zero-copy binding for the iGPU and fault injection before inference. The iGPU then uses the corrupted model for subsequent inferences. We evaluate BridgeHammer on a heterogeneous Intel CPU-iGPU platform using OpenVINO, targeting ResNet-20, VGG-16, and ResNet-50 at both INT8 and FP32 precision. Across all six configurations, BridgeHammer achieves an 88.9% attack success rate (ASR) and 86.3% clean accuracy on average, with reliable target-page placement and bit-flip reproduction. These results demonstrate a new integrity vulnerability on heterogeneous CPU-iGPU SoCs, motivating cross-domain memory integrity protections.

papers.title: Distance from the Truth: Why Fragmented Merchant Underwriting Misses Risk, and What Source-Attributable Evidence Changes
papers.abstract: Merchant underwriting becomes vulnerable when evidence is evaluated without enough visibility into its source, freshness, relationship to the applicant, or meaning for the proposed activity. Individually favorable checks do not necessarily establish that the same business is operating the merchant account, that its representative may bind it, or that its settlement instructions are authorized. We describe three failure modes of fragmented underwriting: distance from the source, the gap between a decision and the evidence needed to justify it; the correlation gap, in which material relationships among the person, legal entity, owners or controllers, representative, business activity, and settlement destination are not evaluated when each signal is considered alone; and point-in-time controls, in which a historical verification is treated as present eligibility. We map these failure modes to identity-proofing, customer-due-diligence, sanctions, third-party-risk, card-network, and Nacha requirements, and propose a merchant-underwriting application of the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture built on provenance, correlation, and persistence. The application keeps a logically unified evidence record that identifies what was checked, the subject and relationship involved, the relevant times, the applicable policy, the decision, and any exceptions, and it keeps evidence validation, applicant verification, organizational authority, and the institution's risk judgment separate. We also set out a proposed evidence and decision receipt, a defined 90-day shadow enrollment pilot with adjudicated outcome measures and deliberate control-failure tests, and a ten-question self-assessment. Proposed controls, illustrative scenarios, and pilot measures are identified as such and are not represented as observed production results.

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.

papers.title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
papers.abstract: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

papers.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines
papers.abstract: The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.

papers.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.

papers.title: SoK: When FL Clients Cannot Train -- Delegated Federated Learning for IoT
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) assumes that a client can perform the computation required to produce its own contribution. This assumption is often unrealistic for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices, motivating designs that delegate some or all client-side training to more capable parties. We systematize this setting as delegated federated learning (Delegated FL), where data ownership and execution of owner-attributed learning are separated. We develop a framework that examines three dimensions over the same delegated transition: delegate-view privacy, delegated attribution, and constrained-owner feasibility. Our audit of 29 systems reveals a recurring composition gap. Privacy mechanisms protect selected artifacts without necessarily characterizing the accumulated view. Attribution mechanisms establish individual execution relations without necessarily binding the complete delegated transition. Furthermore, computational offloading does not establish whether the remaining workload fits the owner's resource budget. Two controlled studies on Raspberry Pi devices illustrate these gaps. We show that encrypted inputs can coexist with information leakage through an exposed residual and that locally retained labels remain inferable from split-learning gradients. We also show that message authentication can reject tampering without establishing that the executor performed the prescribed computation. Our findings demonstrate why individually established guarantees do not necessarily support the same end-to-end claim and motivate evaluating privacy, attribution, and residual owner cost over the same delegated transition.

papers.title: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies
papers.abstract: Face Verification (FV) systems have exhibited remarkable performance in verification tasks and have consequently garnered extensive adoption across various applications, from identity duplication to authentication in mobile payments. However, the surge in popularity of face verification has raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities in the face of adversarial attacks. These concerns originate from the fact that advanced FV systems, which rely on deep neural networks, have recently demonstrated susceptibility to crafted input samples known as adversarial examples. Although imperceptible to human observers, adversarial examples can deceive deep neural networks during the testing and deployment phases. These vulnerabilities raised significant concerns about the deployment of deep neural networks in safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive investigations into adversarial attacks and corresponding defense strategies. This comprehensive survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep face verification, encompassing a broad spectrum of topics such as algorithmic designs, database utilization, protocols, and application scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of state-of-the-art algorithms to generate adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms devised to mitigate such adversarial threats.

papers.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
papers.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

papers.title: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators
papers.abstract: On an FPGA system-on-chip, the software that submits work to an accelerator also decides what the accelerator does. It writes the registers one by one, and the hardware runs whatever it finds, so faulty or compromised software can change one address or resend a job. Existing protections decide who may reach an accelerator or keep its data safe. Deciding whether one job was approved and is still unused takes three things in one place: the only way to the accelerator, the whole job held back until checked, and a record of used approvals. WADJET puts the three in one gate in FPGA logic. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job, with a sequence number, using Ascon-AEAD128. The gate verifies the whole job before releasing any part, accepts only a newer sequence number, uses it up, and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. The gate replaces only the processor's direct line to the registers and works beside the existing protections. In a software model, a check on each write ran jobs mixed from two approved ones; the whole-job rule released none. Its release path is proven on the Verilog for all inputs. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated ones. It needs a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection, which protects more, and adds about ten microseconds to starting a job. It assumes trusted control of its key, reset, and configuration.

papers.title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
papers.abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.

papers.title: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action(VLA) Models Only Through Bit Flips
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions in real-world environments, making malicious model tampering a potential threat to physical safety. We study whether object-triggered backdoors can be implanted through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips without retraining. The central challenge is to make persistent weight modifications disrupt trigger-present behavior while preserving performance on non-trigger inputs. We propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector-amplifier method that exploits existing visual features within an FC-GELU-FC structure. The selector constructs a trigger-dependent response in a selected channel, using GELU to attenuate background activity. The amplifier modifies a connected downstream weight to convert this response into an action-relevant perturbation. Channel screening and discrete bit search construct both components under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22% to 100%, with task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points on clean scenes.

papers.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
papers.abstract: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.

papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.abstract: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.
